transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you in to see me?

Hi. Um, well, I came in because people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain. It's happening a lot with my artist statements and my client notes... oh, and in my meetings. I've been having a lot of meetings lately because I'm trying to secure this new studio space downtown, which has these gorgeous exposed brick walls. I just love brick, it really grounds a room, you know? My current apartment just has this sterile drywall. I tried painting it this warm ochre color last weekend to give it some life, but it still feels so flat. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Right, the meetings. I'll be talking, and my words just start jumping from, like, the physical textures of the materials to the financial budgets, and then to the secret meanings behind the work. It all connects perfectly in my head, but my clients just look at me blankly and say they can't follow my train of thought at all.
Have you found that you need less sleep than usual lately to feel fully rested?

Yeah, actually, that's exactly what's happening. I'll be working late—I've been in this incredible flow state with my art—and I can sleep for just two or three hours and wake up feeling so bright and ready to keep going. I'm not tired at all the way I normally would be. 

It's actually been great because the night is just so quiet. Have you ever noticed how different the streetlights look at, like, 3 AM? The light has this weird, almost bluish-silver quality to it... kind of like the underglaze I’ve been using for my new ceramic pieces. I actually found this amazing local supplier for glazes who sources all his own raw minerals. The guy who runs the shop is a retired geologist, and he was telling me all about how copper carbonate reacts in the kiln when you deprive it of oxygen. It's fascinating, really, how heat just completely transforms the chemical structure of things...
Have you ever had periods in the past where you felt the opposite—extremely down, depressed, or lacking energy?

Extremely down? Um... no, I don't think so. I haven't really noticed feeling like that, lacking energy or anything. I mean, sometimes I feel a little slow if it's been raining for days, but who doesn't? 

Speaking of rain, the roof at my old studio started leaking last month, right over my work table. It was dripping directly onto this massive canvas I was prepping. I use this traditional rabbit skin glue to size my canvases—it's what the Renaissance masters used. You have to heat it up in a double boiler, and honestly, it smells terrible, kind of like wet dog. But the way it tightens the fabric is just incredible, it makes it sound like a drum when you tap it. My neighbor down the hall complained about the smell, though. She makes these intricate little wire sculptures, mostly of crows and ravens. We traded pieces once, actually. Her wire birds are so delicate, they look like they could just fly away if you breathe on them...

Oh, yeah, definitely. There are these stretches where I just feel totally lit up, you know? Like I'm completely unstoppable and every single idea I have is just absolute brilliance. But then, it's weird, because I can be on this amazing high, and a collaborator will say one tiny little thing—like, just a small comment about a piece—and I'll just snap. Like, really snap, in a way that feels way bigger than the situation calls for. 

Like last month with my friend Mark, he just asked if a canvas was dry yet, and I completely bit his head off. But speaking of drying, it is so hard to get oils to cure properly when the humidity is high. I've been experimenting with adding different alkyd mediums to speed up the process. Alkyd is actually a polyester resin, which sounds so synthetic, but it really changes the viscosity of the paint in this beautiful way. It makes it stringy, almost like honey. I get my honey from this local apiary out in the valley, they have these amazing lavender-infused jars. The bees just feed directly on the lavender fields, so the flavor is completely natural, not like that artificial syrup they sell at the grocery store. The beekeeper wears this incredible vintage canvas suit, too, which I've been trying to convince him to let me use for a sculpture... wait, what were you asking about?
How long has this current period of having so much energy and needing so little sleep been going on?

Um, well, this whole thing... these stretches where I'm just buzzing with energy, snapping at people, barely sleeping but working on a million projects at once? It's been going on for about ten months now. 

Ten months... which is actually exactly how long I've been renting my new studio space. It's this incredible loft in an old converted textile mill. The floors are original hardwood, and they have these deep grooves in them from where the heavy machinery used to sit. The landlord was telling me that during the industrial revolution, they used to produce miles and miles of this specific type of woven cotton there. It makes you think about how many hands touched those threads, you know? I've actually been trying to incorporate some woven elements into my mixed media pieces lately to honor the history of the building. I found this amazing vintage loom at an estate sale last weekend. The woman who owned it was 92 and she used to weave her own rugs using scrap fabric. She had this one rug that was entirely made out of old denim jeans... it was so heavy, you wouldn't believe it. I wonder if she ever tried dyeing the denim with natural indigo? Indigo dyeing is such a fascinating process, the way it oxidizes in the air and turns from green to blue...

Um, serious problems? I mean, I guess it depends on how you look at it. I have missed a few paid deadlines recently, which isn't great. And I've definitely confused some of my collaborators during meetings... they just look at me like I'm speaking another language. Oh, and my gallery actually postponed my upcoming exhibition because they said my notes and proposals just weren't making enough sense to use anymore. 

Which is so frustrating, because the proposals were written on this incredible handmade paper I sourced from Japan. It's called Washi paper, and it's made from the inner bark of the gampi tree. The texture is just unbelievable, it's so strong but almost translucent. I've been thinking about using it to create these large-scale illuminated lanterns for my next installation. You know, light completely changes how we perceive space. I was reading this article about bioluminescence in deep-sea creatures, and how they use light to communicate in total darkness. The anglerfish, for example, has this glowing lure... it's actually a symbiotic relationship with bioluminescent bacteria. Bacteria are so fascinating, right? They're everywhere, even inside us, helping us digest food. I tried making my own kombucha a while ago to get more probiotics, but the SCOBY got so huge it took over the whole jar. It looked like this giant, rubbery mushroom floating in tea... wait, what did you ask me about problems?
During this time, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people couldn't see or hear?

Um, voices or seeing things? Yeah, I guess sometimes. Like, when I'm alone in the studio, working late, I'll hear this woman... she's just quietly commenting on things, right from behind the storage shelves. Or sometimes I'll smell this really intense scent of hot metal near an unfinished piece. It feels completely real, like she's right there, but when I go check behind the shelves, there's absolutely nothing. 

Speaking of shelves, I actually built those storage racks myself out of reclaimed scaffolding planks. The wood has these incredible scorch marks and paint splatters from whatever construction site it came from. I love using reclaimed materials, there's just so much history embedded in them. Like this one time I found a whole box of antique glass apothecary bottles at a flea market. The glass was that beautiful, wavy kind with bubbles trapped inside... they call it seeded glass, I think. People used to keep all sorts of tinctures and powders in them, probably some things that were completely toxic by today's standards. Like lead white paint! Did you know Renaissance painters used lead white because it had this unmatched opacity and warmth? But of course, it slowly poisoned them. The history of pigments is so wild, like how they used to make a certain shade of brown by grinding up actual Egyptian mummies. Mummy brown, they called it. Can you imagine painting a portrait with ground-up mummies? I wonder if the resin they used for embalming affected the drying time of the paint... wait, what were we just talking about?

Like my tubes of paint. Especially the cadmium red. Cadmium is a heavy metal, you know, it's incredibly toxic if you ingest it or breathe in the pigment dust. They actually use it in batteries, too. Nickel-cadmium batteries. I remember I had this vintage Walkman that ran on those, and one time the battery acid leaked and completely ruined the inside compartment. It was devastating because I used to listen to this one specific mixtape my sister made me on it, back when you had to sit by the radio and hit record at the exact right second to catch a song. The DJ would always talk over the intro, which used to drive me crazy. Radio DJs have such a specific cadence to their voices, don't they? It's almost like a vocal performance art. I wonder if they take classes for that, or if they just naturally sound like they're trying to sell you a used car... wait, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? The shelves?

Um, substances? No, I don't use anything like that. No drugs or alcohol or anything. I mean, I drink coffee, obviously. I actually have this incredible pour-over setup in the studio. It's a Chemex, which is so beautiful, it looks like a piece of scientific glassware. It was actually designed by a chemist in the 1940s, Peter Schlumbohm. He wanted to make a coffee maker that was perfectly functional but also aesthetically pleasing, and it's even in the permanent collection at MOMA. Museum collections are so fascinating, how they decide what objects are culturally significant enough to preserve forever. Like, who decides that a coffee maker is art, but a toaster isn't? Although, I did see an exhibition once that featured these vintage toasters from the 1920s, and the chrome detailing on them was just stunning. It's like the Art Deco movement touched absolutely everything, even kitchen appliances. The Chrysler Building is probably the most famous example of Art Deco architecture, right? With those gorgeous terraced arches at the top... wait, did you ask me about my coffee?

Um, medical conditions? No, not really. I mean, I'm pretty healthy. I haven't had any major illnesses or anything like that. I did break my wrist once when I was younger, which was a total nightmare because I couldn't paint for months. I had to wear this incredibly bulky fiberglass cast. Did you know they used to use plaster of Paris for casts? It's crazy how heavy those must have been. Plaster of Paris is actually really amazing to work with in the studio, though. You can cast almost anything with it. I made this series of small sculptures once by casting the insides of different fruits. The pomegranate was the most difficult because of all the seeds, but the texture came out looking like something from another planet. Textures are so important in art, don't you think? Like the difference between a matte finish and a high gloss. I always prefer matte because it absorbs the light rather than reflecting it, which makes the colors look so much deeper and richer. Like velvet. Velvet is such a luxurious fabric, historically it was only worn by royalty because it was so expensive to produce. They had to weave it on these special looms... wait, what were you asking me? Did you want to know about my wrist?

Did I have this happening before? Um, yeah, it's actually been going on for about a year and two months now. It started right around the time I switched from community curation into full-time independent installation work. Installation work is so completely different from curation because you're considering the entire spatial environment, not just hanging things on a wall. I had to rent this massive warehouse space just to fit my pieces, and the ceilings are like twenty feet high. Heating a space with twenty-foot ceilings is practically impossible, the heat just rises straight to the top. Hot air is less dense than cold air, right? Basic thermodynamics. I remember taking this physics class in college as an elective, and the professor was completely obsessed with hot air balloons. He actually built a miniature one out of tissue paper and a birthday candle to demonstrate buoyancy in the lecture hall. Buoyancy is such a weird concept when you really think about it, like how those massive steel cargo ships can float just because of the displacement of water. I saw a documentary about how they build those ships, and the scale of the dry docks is just terrifying. I actually have this huge phobia of being near really massive submerged objects. Submechanophobia, I think it's called? It's like when you see a picture of the underside of an iceberg or a sunken submarine and your stomach just drops. The ocean is so incredibly deep and we know less about it than we know about outer space... wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Did you want to know about my warehouse?

Um, negative symptoms? Like... not feeling things? No, I don't think so. I mean, I feel everything, really. Sometimes too much, honestly. Especially when I'm working with certain colors. Like, Prussian Blue is just the most emotionally devastating color to me. It's so deep and melancholic. Did you know it was actually the first modern synthetic pigment? It was discovered completely by accident in Berlin in the early 1700s by this guy trying to make a red pigment. He used some contaminated potash and ended up with this brilliant blue instead. It's wild how many scientific discoveries happen by accident. Like penicillin! Alexander Fleming just left a petri dish out and went on vacation, and when he came back, mold had killed the bacteria. Vacation sounds so nice right now. I haven't been on a real trip in ages. I'd love to go somewhere with really dramatic landscapes, like Iceland. The volcanic rock there is supposed to be incredible, all those jagged basalt columns against the ocean. Basalt is an igneous rock, right? It forms from rapidly cooling lava. I've always wanted to see an active volcano, but it's probably pretty dangerous. The heat alone would be unbearable... wait, what were we talking about? Did you ask about my colors?

Um, yeah, if I look over the whole year and two months, I guess the really energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have definitely taken up more of the time than the calmer periods. Even though the intensity kind of goes up and down, you know? It's like a rollercoaster, but one that's mostly stuck at the top. Rollercoasters are actually fascinating from an engineering standpoint. The way they use potential and kinetic energy to keep the cars moving without an engine on the track itself. It's all gravity and momentum after that first big drop. I went on this one coaster when I was a teenager that had three loops and a corkscrew, and I swear my stomach didn't catch up with my body until I was back in the parking lot. Parking lots are such a waste of urban space, honestly. There's this movement now to tear up asphalt and plant native gardens instead, which I think is brilliant. Asphalt is terrible for the environment, it creates these massive heat islands in cities because it absorbs so much solar radiation. Solar radiation is what makes the colors in my resin sculptures degrade over time if I don't use a UV protectant. UV rays actually break down the chemical bonds in the pigments. It's kind of tragic, really, that light is both what allows us to see the art and what eventually destroys it. It's very poetic, in a destructive way. Like a moth to a flame. Moths are so misunderstood, everyone thinks they're just ugly butterflies, but some of them are incredibly beautiful, like the Luna moth... wait, what were you asking me? Did you want to know about my resin pieces?

I watched this video of a guy who poured a solid block of resin that was like two feet thick, and it got so hot it cracked the mold and started smoking. Anteaters are such bizarre creatures, the way their snouts are shaped and they don't even have teeth. Imagine not having teeth and just swallowing everything whole. I actually had to get my wisdom teeth out last year and it was awful, I couldn't eat solid food for a week... wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Did you ask about my studio?
